title: Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection via Group Sparse Low-Rank Tensor Factorization With Automatic Anomaly Grouping
abstract: Low-rank tensor modeling has become an effective tool for hyperspectral anomaly detection. However, existing methods still suffer from high computational cost and limited flexibility in characterizing spatially structured anomalies. To address these issues, this paper proposes a hyperspectral anomaly detection method based on group sparse low-rank tensor factorization with automatic anomaly grouping (GSAA). Specifically, the low tubal rank background is characterized by imposing group sparsity on tensor factors, which provides an efficient alternative to direct tensor rank regularization. For anomaly modeling, a latent grouping map is introduced to build an automatic anomaly grouping penalty, allowing anomaly groups to be adaptively inferred from the data rather than predefined at the pixel level. To further exploit complementary spectral and spatial information, GSAA is applied in both domains, and the resulting detection maps are fused to form a spectral--spatial version of GSAA, termed GSAA-SS. An efficient linearized alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm with convergence guarantee is developed to solve the resulting model. Experimental results on five real hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior detection performance and competitive computational efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art methods.

title: Belief relevance in the forgetting process of goal-oriented intelligent agents
abstract: An intelligent agent’s belief base grows due to perceptions, communication, and deductions; however, not all of these beliefs remain relevant over time. Forgetting is an important epistemic process for removing information from the agent’s beliefs base with the aim to improve the reasoning computational efficiency. This is particularly important in goals reasoning because beliefs support the progress of goals status during the reasoning cycle. In this article, we endow intelligent agents with the capacity to forget beliefs considered irrelevant. For the forgetting process, we base on the Data-oriented Belief Revision (DBR) model and develop algorithms for the storing, retrieval, and forgetting operations that make part of this process. These operations consider the beliefs relevance; hence, for this calculation we propose to consider a factor that reflects the notion of how long it is left until a goal is achieved. We compare this form of calculation with the most used in literature. To evaluate our proposal and the impact of forgetting on goals processing, we carried out an experiment with two in beliefs-desires-intention agents (BDI) and belief-based goal processing agents (BBGP). The results of the experiment showed that our proposal leads to an improvement in processing efficiency and memory efficiency in most of the evaluated situations.

title: A classroom concentration detection method based on deep learning image analysis
abstract: The precise perception of students’ concentration in the classroom is the core foundation of intelligent teaching analysis and learning situation assessment. Traditional methods of observing students’ learning situations through manual observation or questionnaire surveys have drawbacks such as strong subjectivity, poor real-time performance, high labor costs, and difficulty in adapting to large-scale classroom scenarios. The existing deep learning detection methods mostly rely solely on facial expression features, ignoring the correlation of multi-dimensional classroom visual information such as head posture and body behavior, resulting in issues such as weak anti-interference ability in complex classroom environments, and insufficient accuracy of concentration classification. To address these problems, this paper proposes a classroom concentration detection method based on multi-feature fusion of deep learning images. Firstly, for complex interference scenarios such as variable classroom lighting, character occlusion, and perspective deviation, a multidimensional classroom visual feature system including students’ facial states, head postures, and body movements is constructed to improve the feature dimensions for concentration determination; Secondly, a lightweight attention mechanism is introduced to optimize the feature extraction network, strengthening the weight response of effective learning situation features, suppressing background noise and invalid interference information, and solving the problems of redundant features in traditional models and insufficient extraction of key learning situation information; Finally, based on the learning cognitive laws of the classroom, a multi-level concentration quantitative discrimination criterion is constructed to achieve refined classification detection of different learning states such as high concentration, general engagement, and distraction. Experiments are conducted using a large-scale annotated dataset collected from real classrooms, and the results show that compared with mainstream baseline models, this method has significantly improved the accuracy and robustness of concentration detection in complex classroom scenarios. This method can effectively complement the shortcomings of traditional learning situation monitoring methods and provide reliable technical support and data support for intelligent classroom learning situation assessment, personalized teaching intervention, and quality improvement of teaching.

title: Amplification of bosonic interactions through squeezing in the presence of decoherence
abstract: We consider the amplification of bosonic interactions through parametric control that implements squeezing along orthogonal quadratures. We show that bosonic interactions described by certain classes of quadratic and quartic Hamiltonians can be enhanced in this way while simultaneously overcoming noise and decoherence. In general, the amplification method enhances both desired and undesired interactions present in the system. Depending on the case, however, detrimental processes can be less amplified than the desired couplings. We leverage this observation to improve the fidelity for preparing Bell-type entangled states between two bosonic modes in the presence of noise and losses. We also investigate noise models for which the protocol either fails or partially achieves a loss-tolerant state preparation speedup. Our work facilitates faster preparation of complex quantum states and implementation of entangling gates in the presence of decoherence mechanisms.
